The side project principle also connects to the importance of maintaining multiple creative projects at different stages simultaneously. When you are blocked on one project, you can make progress on another. When one project is in the painful, unglamorous middle — past the exciting beginning but far from the satisfying end — another project can provide the novelty and excitement that keeps you going. Kleon recommends always having something new and something finished in progress at the same time: something to be excited about and something to complete.

summarySections.heading: The Internet as creative resource and creative threat
paragraphs: Kleon addresses the internet with nuance that is often missing in conversations about creativity and technology. The internet is, he argues, an extraordinary resource for the practices he advocates: finding your influences' influences, sharing work in progress, building an audience before you're ready, and encountering creative work from contexts and traditions you would never otherwise find. The amateur internet — the world of blogs, social media posts, and self-published work — is a massive archive of creative process that previous generations of artists could only have dreamed of accessing.

At the same time, the always-on nature of the internet is a genuine threat to the sustained, distraction-free attention that creative work requires. Kleon advocates a practice he calls 'disconnecting to connect' — deliberately going offline during periods of deep creative work, not as a permanent rejection of the internet but as a recognition that the internet's mode of attention (perpetual switching between short, stimulating inputs) is incompatible with the creative mode of attention (sustained engagement with a single problem).

His practical prescription is having two desks or two computers: one connected (for research, sharing, communication, and inspiration) and one disconnected (for actual creative work). The physical separation creates a spatial cue that supports the attentional shift between modes. This may sound like an extreme solution, but Kleon argues that the attention required for genuine creative work — the slow, sustained, tolerant-of-boredom engagement with difficult material — is sufficiently different from the attention the internet demands that they cannot be maintained simultaneously.

summarySections.heading: Geography, community, and the creative environment
paragraphs: Kleon addresses the role of place and community in creative work with an interesting tension. On one hand, he argues for the specific value of creative communities — clusters of people working in related fields, sharing work, providing feedback, and generating the kind of productive competition and inspiration that is hard to find in isolation. The creative explosion of specific cities, specific neighborhoods, and specific historical moments — Greenwich Village in the 1960s, Silicon Valley in the 1990s, the Bloomsbury Group in the 1920s — was not accidental; it was the product of genuine community.

On the other hand, he argues that the internet has made creative community portable in ways that partially decouple it from geography. The creative community you need is increasingly findable online, and the important relationships — with people who do related work, who challenge you, who share your sensibility — can be maintained across distance in ways that were impossible before. He recommends building your internet presence as if you live in the city where your creative community is, even if you physically live far from it.

His final advice about community is characteristically practical: surround yourself with people who are smarter than you, who make you better, and who challenge your work honestly rather than flattering you. The creative environment that produces the best work is not the one that makes you feel most comfortable; it is the one that makes you most ambitious, most rigorous, and most willing to fail in the service of making something genuinely good.

summarySections.heading: Final summary
paragraphs: Steal Like an Artist is a slim, visually beautiful book that can be read in an hour and thought about for months. It will not give you a systematic creative process — that is not what it is for. It will give you permission: permission to borrow freely from the work that has inspired you, to start before you are ready, to share imperfect work in progress, to be boring and scheduled and stable, to cultivate the side project, to follow genuine curiosity wherever it leads.

Kleon's gift is a relaxed attitude toward creativity at a time when creative paralysis — the inability to start or share work because it might not be good enough — is endemic. The cure for creative paralysis, in his view, is never to think harder or be more original. It is to steal more widely, start more recklessly, and care less about whether your influences are showing. The most original work comes from the most thoroughly saturated creators — people who have consumed so much that their influences have become invisible, transformed into a voice that is genuinely their own.

Read it when you are feeling stuck. Read it when you are comparing yourself unfavorably to people whose work you admire. Read it when you are waiting to start until you feel ready. Kleon's consistent message, on every page, is the same: you are ready. Start. The stealing, the sharing, the learning, and the making are all the same practice, and the practice begins with permission.

title: The Art and Business of Online Writing
author: Nicolas Cole
shortDescription: Nicolas Cole went from gaming forums to one of the most-read writers on the internet, then built a business teaching others how. His step-by-step guide to building an audience by writing online — the platform, the craft, and the economics.
keyTakeaways: Write for the reader's benefit, not for self-expression. The question is always: why does this matter to the reader?
Powerful openers — the first line decides everything. The reader decides whether to continue in seconds.
Categories of content: opinions, how-tos, lists, and stories. Understanding which one you're writing shapes structure immediately.
Build an audience before you need one. Consistent publishing compounds over time like interest.
The secret to online writing: prove you can be interesting about the obvious. The hardest topics are the familiar ones.

summarySections.heading: How Cole became a writer — and what that reveals about online platforms
paragraphs: Nicolas Cole's origin story as a writer is unusual and instructive. He began writing online not on a literary platform but on a gaming forum, crafting long analyses of game mechanics, player psychology, and competitive strategy for an audience of fellow gamers who were deeply invested in the subject. This experience taught him something that most writing teachers miss: the rules of compelling online writing were the same regardless of the topic. What kept a gamer reading an analysis of a competitive strategy was exactly what keeps a business reader reading a marketing case study: a clear argument, specific evidence, a narrative arc, and a payoff.

He went on to build a substantial audience on Quora, becoming one of the most-read writers on that platform, and then replicated that success on Medium, LinkedIn, and his own newsletter. The patterns he identified across these different platforms became the framework for this book: a systematic, empirically tested set of principles for writing that actually gets read, shared, and remembered on the internet, as opposed to writing that simply exists there.

The book is unusual in its combination of craft and business. Most writing books focus on either the art (how to write well) or the business (how to monetize your writing). Cole treats these as inseparable: the craft of online writing — the specific techniques that make people read, share, and return — is itself the business strategy, because everything else (audience, reputation, platform, revenue) flows from the quality and consistency of the work itself.

summarySections.heading: Why online writing is different — and what those differences require
paragraphs: Cole's foundational argument is that online writing operates under fundamentally different conditions than academic writing, journalism, or books, and that applying the conventions of those other forms to online writing is one of the most common causes of online writing failure. In an academic essay, the reader is captive — they have an assignment to complete or a grade to receive. In a print magazine, the design and the physical object create a default engagement. Online, the reader is free to leave at any point, has dozens of alternative tabs open, and has a conditioned expectation of immediate value.

This radical freedom from captive readership has specific implications for every structural choice the online writer makes. The opening line must earn the second. The second sentence must earn the third. The first paragraph must justify the second. There is no 'building toward the point' — the point must be available from the beginning, not as a conclusion but as a promise: here is why the next three minutes of your attention will be worth something. The reader doesn't owe you their attention; you earn it, sentence by sentence.

The practical consequence is that online writing requires a fundamentally different set of structural instincts than other forms. The traditional essayistic convention of establishing context before making an argument, of warming up to the point through background and qualification, is precisely wrong for online reading. The online reader needs the argument first, the context later, and the qualification only if it genuinely serves the argument. This inversion of conventional structure is one of the hardest adjustments for writers trained in academic or print conventions to make.

summarySections.heading: The power of the opening — the first line decides everything
paragraphs: Cole devotes more attention to opening lines than to any other single element of craft, and for good reason: the research on online reading behavior consistently shows that the first sentence determines whether the second is read, and the second determines whether the third is read, and so on. The reader makes an initial judgment about whether this piece of writing is worth their time in the first two to five seconds. The first line is the mechanism of that judgment.

He categorizes effective opening types: the surprising statement ('Most people who exercise regularly are doing it wrong'), the counterintuitive claim ('The best advice I ever received I initially rejected entirely'), the specific detail that implies a rich world ('On the morning I made my first $10,000 online, I was sitting in a McDonald's in suburban Chicago at 7am'), and the direct question that places the reader inside a dilemma they recognize ('Have you ever finished a long day of hard work and felt completely empty?'). Each type works by a different mechanism, and each is appropriate for a different kind of content.

The common thread across all effective openings is tension: they create a gap between where the reader is and where the writer is promising to take them. The surprising statement creates a tension between the reader's existing belief and what the writer is claiming. The counterintuitive claim creates intellectual curiosity. The specific detail creates narrative interest. The direct question creates personal relevance. Any opening that reduces rather than creates tension — that begins with reassurance, context-setting, or qualification — fails to earn the reader's continued attention.

summarySections.heading: Content categories and structural logic
paragraphs: Cole argues that all effective online content falls into a small number of structural categories, and that identifying which category you're writing determines the structural logic that makes the piece work. The four major categories are: opinions (a specific, arguable claim about how the world works or should work), how-tos (a process the reader can follow to achieve a specific result), lists (a collection of related insights, examples, or items organized around a shared theme), and stories (a specific personal experience that demonstrates a general truth).

Each category has a different structural logic. Opinions require a clear thesis in the first paragraph, evidence and reasoning in the body, and a restatement that shows why the argument matters. How-tos require a specific, achievable outcome in the opening, a sequence of steps that the reader can actually follow, and specificity at every stage (not 'be more organized' but 'create a physical inbox on your desk for all pending tasks'). Lists require a clear theme, consistent level of abstraction across items, and enough items to feel comprehensive without becoming exhausting. Stories require the storytelling craft that Dicks and others have described.

The most common online writing failure is structural category confusion: an opinion that tries to also be a how-to, a list that meanders into personal story, a how-to that becomes an opinion about why the how-to matters. Each confusion makes the piece less useful for the reader who came for a specific kind of content and harder to share because its purpose is unclear. Clarity about category is not a constraint on creativity; it is the scaffolding that makes creativity possible.

summarySections.heading: Building an audience — the compound interest of consistent publishing
paragraphs: Cole's growth strategy is deliberately unsexy: publish consistently, in one place, on a defined schedule. He is not talking about going viral — viral is unpredictable, cannot be manufactured, and produces a spike of attention that typically doesn't convert into lasting audience. He is talking about compound interest. The writer who publishes 300 pieces over three years has 300 individual pieces of content in the world, each of which may find new readers at any time. The writer who publishes 3 pieces does not have 1/100 of the audience of the 300-piece writer; they have an audience in the hundreds while the other writer may have hundreds of thousands.

He also emphasizes the importance of niche: the writer who writes about everything is remembered for nothing. The writer who becomes the definitive voice on a specific topic, perspective, or intersection of interests builds a recognizable identity that readers seek out and return to. This doesn't mean staying in a narrow lane forever; it means being specific enough to be memorable in the early stages of audience-building, and then expanding from a position of established credibility rather than from ambiguity.

The compound interest metaphor extends to quality as well as quantity. The writer who publishes consistently is also improving consistently — they are in a continuous cycle of feedback from audience response, which teaches them what resonates and what doesn't, what formats work for their particular audience, and what topics they can cover more authoritatively. The improvement compounds alongside the audience: the 300th piece is typically much better than the first, which means the writer at the end of the process is not just more visible but more skilled.

summarySections.heading: The business of writing — monetization and leverage
paragraphs: Cole is unusually concrete about the economics of online writing, which most writing books treat either with complete silence or with vague gestures toward 'monetization.' His argument is that the business of online writing follows the same principle as the craft: it is about providing value at scale, and the revenue follows from the audience and reputation that consistent, high-quality writing builds over time.

He describes several monetization paths: paid newsletters (readers pay directly for continued access to your writing), digital products (courses, ebooks, templates, tools built from your expertise and sold to your audience), sponsorships and brand partnerships (companies pay to reach your audience through your content), consulting and services (your audience and reputation generate client inquiries for your professional expertise), and books (traditional or self-published works that consolidate and extend your online presence).

The common thread across all these paths is that they flow from an established audience and reputation — which flows from consistent, high-quality writing. This means the order of operations is clear: write well and consistently for long enough to build an audience, then decide how to monetize that audience. Trying to monetize before building the audience produces poor results and often compromises the writing quality that is the foundation of the whole enterprise. The business follows the craft; the craft doesn't follow the business.

summarySections.heading: Final summary
paragraphs: The Art and Business of Online Writing is a practical, no-nonsense guide aimed directly at people who want to build an audience on the internet — not to become literary novelists, not to impress academic audiences, but to communicate ideas effectively to real readers who have chosen to be there and can leave at any moment. It assumes that goal as given and provides the most direct path to it that Cole's extensive experience can offer.

Cole's central gift is his refusal to mystify the process. Good online writing is a craft, not a talent. It can be studied, broken down into component skills, practiced systematically, and improved measurably. The principles he articulates — about opening lines, structural categories, audience specificity, consistent publishing — are not personal opinions but empirically tested observations about what actually works in the specific environment of online reading.

The internet rewards people who show up, improve, and keep going. That is the simplest summary of everything in this book, and it is simultaneously the most difficult thing to do and the most available to anyone willing to start. Cole's experience is proof that the path from unknown to widely-read is traversable through consistent, skilled work over time — not through a single viral post, not through the right connection or the right credential, but through the accumulation of good work published consistently for long enough to compound.
